Common Infusion Center Billing Problems

Each problem below is one PMEX resolves before it costs you revenue.

Drug quantity billed at vial size rather than the actual administered dose from the nursing record.

PMEX verifies administered dose from the infusion nursing record and calculates the correct J-code billing units.

Sequential infusion code used when concurrent timing makes concurrent coding correct.

PMEX reviews infusion start and stop times from the nursing record before assigning sequential vs. concurrent codes.

Biosimilar substituted at pharmacy but branded J-code submitted on the claim.

PMEX tracks biosimilar dispensing and applies the correct Q-code when a biosimilar is administered.

Prior authorization expires between infusion cycles, generating retroactive denial.

PMEX tracks biologic auth expiration and initiates renewal 14 days before the next scheduled infusion.

Hydration billed during concurrent therapeutic infusion when bundling rules prohibit it.

PMEX applies CMS hydration bundling rules and bills hydration separately only when timing and indication support it.

IV push not billed on visits where a drug was administered as a push alongside an infusion.

PMEX identifies push administrations from the nursing record and submits the correct 96374 to 96376 code.

Denial Management

Top Denial Patterns in Infusion Therapy Billing

Infusion centers lose 18 to 30 percent of revenue to drug quantity errors, biosimilar coding mistakes, and authorization gaps on high-cost agents.

PATTERN 01

Drug Quantity Billed at Vial Size, Not Administered Dose

Patient receives 480mg pembrolizumab. J2357 is billed per 1mg. Correct units: 480. Billing team submits 200 (vial size). More than half the drug revenue lost on every infusion with this error. At $30 per unit, that is $8,400 under-billed on a single infusion visit.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX calculates J-code billing units from the administered dose in the infusion nursing record on every infusion claim. Administered dose is confirmed from the nursing documentation, not from the pharmacy order or vial size.

PATTERN 02

Biosimilar Administered, Branded J-Code Submitted

Pharmacy substitutes bevacizumab biosimilar (Mvasi). Claim submitted with J9035 (branded bevacizumab). Correct code: Q5107 (bevacizumab-awwb biosimilar). Payer adjudicates at wrong rate or denies for incorrect J-code. Compliance exposure created.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX tracks biosimilar substitution from the pharmacy dispensing record and applies the correct Q-code for the specific biosimilar administered on every infusion claim, updated as FDA biosimilar approvals expand.

PATTERN 03

Biologic Authorization Expired, Infusion Denied

Patient on 8-week infliximab cycle. Commercial authorization covers 4 infusions. Fifth infusion administered without renewal. Drug claim ($3,200) and administration fee denied retroactively. Renewal application not initiated before the authorization period ended.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX tracks biologic authorization end dates and covered cycle counts per patient and initiates renewal 14 days before the authorization expires, with clinical documentation of treatment response attached from the treating physician notes.

Questions

Infusion Therapy Billing Questions Answered

We verify the administered dose from the infusion nursing record and divide by the per-unit descriptor in the J-code definition. For example, J2357 (pembrolizumab) is billed per 1mg, so a 480mg dose bills as 480 units. We never use the vial size as the billing quantity.

Sequential infusion (separate drug administered after the first drug is completed) uses 96417 for each additional drug. Concurrent infusion (second drug infused at the same time as the first) uses a different code. We confirm timing from the nursing record before coding.

Q-codes are HCPCS codes assigned to FDA-approved biosimilar drugs. When a biosimilar is dispensed instead of the branded biologic, the Q-code for the specific biosimilar replaces the J-code for the branded drug.

It depends on timing and clinical indication. When hydration is administered before or after a therapeutic infusion for a distinct clinical reason, it may be separately billable. When concurrent with a therapeutic infusion during the same time period, it is generally bundled per CMS rules.

Yes. We manage prior authorization for all high-cost biologics, specialty drugs, and infusion therapies, tracking authorization expiration and initiating renewal before each cycle.

Within 30 days, with drug quantity verification, biosimilar tracking, and authorization management active from day one.
